title: 10 — Orchestration, Quality and Governance
html:
10 — Orchestration, Quality and Governance

The one idea: a pipeline that runs is not the same as data you can trust. Orchestration makes pipelines run in the right order and recover from failure; quality checks prove the output is fit for use; governance controls who may see it and proves where it came from. Skip any one of the three and consumers eventually stop believing the numbers.

1. Orchestration: what an orchestrator does

An orchestrator decides what runs, when, in what order, with which parameters, and what happens when something fails. It should not do the heavy data processing itself; it tells Spark, SQL warehouses or other services to do it.

---
title: A daily orchestration DAG with a quality gate
---
flowchart LR
    S["Sensor / trigger<br/>source files arrived"] --> I1["Ingest orders<br/>to bronze"]
    S --> I2["Ingest customers<br/>to bronze"]
    I1 --> T1["Silver orders<br/>(merge)"]
    I2 --> T2["Silver customers<br/>(SCD2)"]
    T1 --> G["Gold sales mart"]
    T2 --> G
    G --> Q{"Quality checks<br/>pass?"}
    Q -->|"yes"| P["Publish: refresh BI,<br/>notify consumers"]
    Q -->|"no"| A["Alert on-call,<br/>do not publish"]

Core concepts

Concept What it means in practice
DAG Tasks and their dependencies. No cycles. The orchestrator runs tasks as soon as their upstreams succeed, in parallel where possible.
Dependencies Within a DAG (task → task) and across DAGs (wait for another pipeline's output). Prefer data-aware triggers (table updated, file arrived) over "run at 03:00 and hope upstream finished at 02:00".
Retries Automatic re-runs of a failed task, with a delay/backoff. Only safe if the task is idempotent. Separate transient failures (network, spot eviction) from logic failures (bad data) — retrying a logic failure just wastes compute.
Idempotent tasks Re-running a task for the same inputs and parameters produces the same result. Achieved with overwrite-by-partition or keyed merges, never blind appends.
Parameters Every task receives its logical date / date range / environment as parameters instead of calling now(). This is what makes backfills and reruns reproducible.
Backfills Running the DAG for past logical dates. The orchestrator should let you run a date range with controlled concurrency.
SLAs A promise that data is ready by a time (e.g. gold sales by 07:00). Orchestrators can alert when a task or run exceeds its expected duration or misses the deadline.
Timeouts Kill a task that runs far longer than normal, so a hung job does not hold resources or block the SLA silently.
Notifications On failure, on SLA miss, and on recovery. Route to the owning team, not a shared inbox nobody reads.

Logical date vs run time

A crucial orchestration idea (Airflow makes it explicit): a run has a logical date — the period of data it is responsible for — which is different from when it actually runs. The run on 2026-09-25 at 02:00 processes data for 2026-09-24. If it fails and you rerun it on 2026-09-27, it must still process 2026-09-24. Pass the logical date as a parameter; never derive it from the clock inside the task.

2. Orchestrators compared

Databricks Workflows (Lakeflow Jobs) Apache Airflow Azure Data Factory
Definition UI, JSON/YAML via API, Asset Bundles Python DAG files UI with JSON definitions, ARM/Bicep, Git integration
Strength Native to Databricks: notebooks, pipelines, SQL, dbt tasks; lineage; repair runs; no extra infrastructure Orchestrates anything with a huge operator ecosystem; code-first; mature backfill model Many connectors, copy activity for bulk movement, integration with Azure networking (self-hosted integration runtime for on-prem)
Weakness Best when most work is in Databricks You run and scale it (or use a managed service); scheduler overhead Complex logic is awkward in the UI; code review of JSON is painful
Triggers Cron, file arrival, table update, continuous, API Cron, datasets (data-aware), sensors, API Schedule, tumbling window, storage events, custom events
Backfill Run with parameters over a range, for-each tasks First-class (airflow dags backfill, catchup) Tumbling window triggers support re-runs over past windows
Typical use Pipelines living in Databricks Multi-system estates Ingestion from many sources into ADLS, and Azure-centric orchestration

A common Azure pattern: ADF (or Lakeflow Connect) copies data from on-premises and SaaS sources into ADLS; Databricks Jobs handle everything from bronze onward. Avoid splitting orchestration of one logical pipeline across two tools unless there is a clear reason — debugging cross-tool dependencies is painful.

An Airflow DAG calling Databricks, showing parameters and retries:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.providers.databricks.operators.databricks import DatabricksRunNowOperator

with DAG(
    dag_id="sales_daily",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    schedule="0 2 * * *",
    catchup=False,
    default_args={"retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=10)},
) as dag:
    run_job = DatabricksRunNowOperator(
        task_id="run_sales_job",
        databricks_conn_id="databricks_prod",
        job_id=123456,
        job_parameters={"run_date": "{{ ds }}"},   # logical date, not wall-clock date
    )

3. Data quality dimensions

Dimension Question Example check
Accuracy Does the data reflect reality / the source? Reconcile daily revenue with the finance system within 0.1%
Completeness Is everything that should be there present? Row count vs source count; email null rate below 2%
Consistency Do related values agree across tables and time? Every fact_sales.customer_key exists in dim_customer; totals match between silver and gold
Timeliness Is it fresh enough? max(_ingested_at) within the last 2 hours
Uniqueness Are there duplicates? order_id unique in silver.orders
Validity Does each value conform to the rules? amount >= 0, currency in allowed list, dates parse, emails match a pattern

Where checks live

Level Tooling Behaviour on failure
Row-level expectations Declarative pipeline expectations, CHECK constraints on Delta tables Keep and log, drop, quarantine or fail
Table-level tests dbt tests, Great Expectations, custom SQL assertions, Databricks data quality monitoring Fail the task or warn
Cross-system reconciliation Custom jobs comparing counts/sums with the source Alert; block publishing 
-- Delta constraints: enforced on every write
ALTER TABLE prod.silver.orders ALTER COLUMN order_id SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE prod.silver.orders ADD CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount >= 0);

Quarantine rather than drop

Dropping bad rows silently hides problems; failing the whole pipeline for one bad row punishes every consumer. The middle path is a quarantine table:

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

rules = {
    "missing_order_id": F.col("order_id").isNull(),
    "negative_amount":  F.col("amount") < 0,
    "bad_currency":     ~F.col("currency").isin("GBP", "EUR", "USD"),
}

# Build an array of failed rule names per row
failed = F.array_compact(F.array(*[F.when(cond, F.lit(name)) for name, cond in rules.items()]))
checked = batch.withColumn("dq_failures", failed)

good = checked.filter(F.size("dq_failures") == 0).drop("dq_failures")
bad  = (checked.filter(F.size("dq_failures") > 0)
        .withColumn("quarantined_at", F.current_timestamp()))

good.write.mode("append").saveAsTable("prod.silver.orders_valid")   # or MERGE
bad.write.mode("append").saveAsTable("prod.quarantine.orders")

Then alert when the quarantine rate exceeds a threshold, and give the source owner a way to see and fix their rejected rows.

4. Data contracts

A data contract is a versioned agreement between a producer and its consumers. It turns "please don't change that column" into something reviewable and testable.

A contract typically specifies:

Section Contents
Ownership Producing team, contact, escalation
Schema Fields, types, nullability, keys, allowed values
Semantics What each field means, units, time zone, how deletes are represented
Quality Uniqueness, completeness thresholds, validation rules
Service levels Freshness (e.g. available within 15 minutes), availability, retention
Change policy What counts as breaking, notice period, versioning (e.g. new major version as a new topic/table) 
# orders.contract.yaml (illustrative format)
name: orders
version: 2.1.0
owner: checkout-team
schema:
  - { name: order_id,    type: string,        required: true, unique: true }
  - { name: customer_id, type: string,        required: true }
  - { name: amount,      type: decimal(18,2), required: true, check: ">= 0" }
  - { name: currency,    type: string,        allowed: [GBP, EUR, USD] }
  - { name: event_time,  type: timestamp,     required: true, timezone: UTC }
sla:
  freshness_minutes: 15
breaking_changes: "new major version, 30 days notice"

Enforce contracts at the boundary: schema registry compatibility checks for events, CI checks on producer schemas, and validation at bronze → silver.

5. Data observability

Tests catch what you anticipated. Observability watches for what you did not. The five commonly cited signals:

Signal Watches Example alert
Freshness When the table last updated gold.sales not updated for 3 hours (normally hourly)
Volume Row counts per load Today's load is 40% below the 4-week same-weekday average
Schema Columns and types Column discount disappeared from the source
Distribution Value statistics: null rates, ranges, cardinality country null rate jumped from 0.1% to 25%
Lineage Upstream and downstream dependencies Show which dashboards are affected by the failed table 
# A simple freshness check using the Delta transaction history
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

last_write = (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "prod.gold.sales").history()
              .filter(F.col("operation").isin("WRITE", "MERGE", "STREAMING UPDATE"))
              .agg(F.max("timestamp").alias("last_write"))
              .first()["last_write"])

lag_minutes = spark.sql(
    f"SELECT timestampdiff(MINUTE, TIMESTAMP'{last_write}', current_timestamp()) AS m"
).first()["m"]

if lag_minutes > 120:
    raise RuntimeError(f"prod.gold.sales is stale: last write {lag_minutes} minutes ago")

A failing check that raises an error fails the task, which triggers the job's normal failure notifications.

On Databricks, data quality monitoring (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring) can profile tables over time and generate drift metrics, and system tables expose job runs, lineage and billing for building your own observability dashboards.

6. Governance

6.1 Catalog and discoverability

Every table should have an owner, a description, column comments and tags (domain, sensitivity, layer). Unity Catalog stores these and makes them searchable; an estate-wide catalogue (e.g. Microsoft Purview) can aggregate across platforms.

COMMENT ON TABLE prod.gold.customers IS 'One row per customer, current state. Owner: customer-data team.';
ALTER TABLE prod.gold.customers ALTER COLUMN email COMMENT 'Primary email, lower-cased';
ALTER TABLE prod.gold.customers SET TAGS ('domain' = 'customer', 'contains_pii' = 'true');
ALTER TABLE prod.gold.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET TAGS ('pii' = 'email');

6.2 Lineage

Lineage answers where did this come from (debugging, trust) and what depends on this (impact analysis before a change). Unity Catalog captures table and column lineage automatically for workloads on UC-enabled compute. Lineage from outside tools (e.g. an external orchestrator or BI tool) may need integration or manual registration.

6.3 Access control

Principles:

  • Least privilege: grant SELECT on gold to analysts; restrict bronze and silver to engineers and service principals.
  • Groups, not individuals, managed from the identity provider (Entra ID).
  • Service principals for production jobs; no personal credentials in pipelines.
  • Environment isolation: developers read prod gold (maybe) but never write to prod; prod jobs never read dev.

Access-control patterns:

Pattern Mechanism
Table / schema / catalog permissions GRANT ... ON ... TO group
Row-level security Row filter functions on tables
Column-level security Column masks, or views exposing only allowed columns
Attribute-based policies Tag-driven policies (e.g. mask all columns tagged pii) where the platform supports them
Dynamic views Views using is_account_group_member() or current_user() in logic

6.4 PII classification and masking

  1. Classify: identify PII columns (manually, and with automated classification/scanning where available). Tag them.
  2. Minimise: don't carry PII into gold unless a use case needs it. Many analytics need a stable pseudonymous key, not a name.
  3. Protect:
Technique Reversible? Use for
Masking (j***@example.com) No (at query time; data unchanged underneath) Showing partial values to support staff
Hashing (SHA-256 with a secret salt/pepper) Not practically, if salted Joinable pseudonymous keys
Tokenisation Yes, via a secure token vault When some systems must recover the original
Encryption (column-level) Yes, with the key Highly sensitive fields; key management per subject enables crypto-shredding

6.5 Retention

Define retention per layer and data type, and implement it:

  • Bronze raw data: long enough to rebuild silver (e.g. 90 days to a few years), constrained by PII rules.
  • Silver/gold: per business and regulatory need.
  • Delta history: delta.logRetentionDuration and delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration, plus scheduled VACUUM.
  • Raw files in storage: storage lifecycle policies (move to cool/archive, then delete).

6.6 GDPR right to erasure in a lakehouse

Erasing a person from a lakehouse is harder than DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 42, because copies exist in many layers and in table history.

---
title: Right-to-erasure workflow in a lakehouse
---
flowchart TB
    R["Erasure request<br/>subject id"] --> L["Lineage lookup:<br/>every table holding the subject"]
    L --> D1["DELETE / anonymise in<br/>bronze, silver, gold"]
    D1 --> P["Purge soft-deleted rows<br/>REORG ... APPLY (PURGE)"]
    P --> V["VACUUM after retention window<br/>removes old file versions"]
    V --> X["Downstream copies:<br/>exports, ML features, caches"]
    X --> C["Record completion<br/>(audit log without the PII)"]

Practical design choices that make erasure feasible:

  • Keep PII in as few tables as possible, joined by a pseudonymous key elsewhere. Then erasure touches a small number of tables.
  • Crypto-shredding: encrypt PII with a per-subject key stored separately; deleting the key renders every copy (including history and backups) unreadable.
  • Bronze retention short enough that raw data containing PII ages out within the legal deadline, or apply deletes to bronze too.
  • Account for time travel: a deleted row is recoverable until VACUUM removes the old files, and with deletion vectors the row stays in its Parquet file until the file is rewritten. Run REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) and VACUUM within the deadline.
  • Change Data Feed also retains the deleted values until files are vacuumed.
  • Track downstream copies: extracts sent to partners, ML training sets, and caches are part of the obligation.

Azure / .NET mapping

Concern Azure option
Orchestration Databricks Jobs; Azure Data Factory / Fabric Data Factory; Managed Airflow options
Identity and access Microsoft Entra ID groups synced to Databricks; service principals with workload identity federation for CI/CD
Catalog across the estate Microsoft Purview (can scan Azure Databricks Unity Catalog)
Secrets and keys Azure Key Vault; customer-managed keys for storage and workspace encryption
Retention of raw files ADLS lifecycle management policies
Alerting Job notifications to Teams/email/webhooks; Azure Monitor alerts

For .NET producers, a data contract fits naturally as a shared schema package (e.g. Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema generated types) versioned in CI, with compatibility checks against the schema registry before a producer can deploy.

Review checklist

  • My tasks are idempotent and take a logical date parameter instead of reading the clock.
  • I can explain retries, backfills, SLAs and timeouts in my orchestrator.
  • I can choose between Workflows, Airflow and Data Factory for a given estate.
  • I can name the six data quality dimensions with one check for each.
  • Bad rows go to a quarantine table with a reason, and quarantine rates are alerted on.
  • Important sources have a data contract with schema, semantics, SLAs and a change policy.
  • I monitor freshness, volume, schema and distribution for key tables.
  • Access is granted to groups, least-privilege, with row filters/masks where needed.
  • PII is classified, tagged, minimised and protected.
  • I can explain how to erase a person from a Delta-based lakehouse, including history.
